verdicts.why: Enforcing a rule is named plainly; the word takes no side on the rule or the enforcer.
Applying oneself to a task is described, not praised or mocked; it is the plain neighbour of its own synonyms.
Applying a word or name to something is a neutral act of reference with no attitude attached.
Applying to someone for consent or help, as the Austen sentences show, is formal but carries no judgement of either party.
A distinction that applies to books is simply relevant to them; the word describes scope, not attitude.
Applying paint or a dressing is a physical action named without approval or contempt.
Giving notice of leaving an arrangement is a plain contractual term; the word neither blames nor excuses.
A posted sign is a thing, and the word for it carries no view of it.
A short review may be kind or harsh, but calling it a notice says nothing about which.
A request for payment is an unwelcome referent, but the word itself is the plain, official name for it.
A symptom of a drug or illness is named without any attitude; the unpleasantness belongs to the referent, not the word.
A law being in effect is a legal state described in plain terms with no judgement of the law.
Words to the effect of something name the gist of a speech without praising or dismissing it.
Inviting someone to attend is a plain social act; the sentences show it used of both welcome and unwelcome guests without the word shifting.
Inviting criticism or comparison leans on a bad or neutral referent, but the word states that something makes an outcome likely and does not itself pass judgement on the subject.
Asking someone to come in is described, not evaluated.
Expressing willingness to have someone in one's home is a plain statement of hospitality, not a judgement of the host or guest.
Having someone as a guest is neutral fact; the word adds no attitude toward either party.
Changing clothes is a bare everyday action with nothing to approve or disapprove of in the word.
Exchanging one thing for another of the same kind is the plainest possible verb for the act.
Changing jobs or sides is stated without the reproach that a word like desert or abandon would carry.
Changing places or words with someone is reciprocal exchange described neutrally.
Changing trains is a routine travel action with no attitude in the word.
A voice or colour that changes is described as altering, and the word does not say whether for better or worse.
